title: Foxes and Hedgehogs
text:
Starting in the mid-1980s, the psychologist Philip Tetlock asked hundreds of experts who made their living commenting on politics and economics to make specific predictions. Would a given leader still be in power in five years? Would a country's economy grow or shrink? Would a border dispute turn into war? The experts included academics, government advisers and journalists. Over roughly two decades he collected tens of thousands of forecasts and then checked them against what actually happened.

The results, published in 2005 in the book Expert Political Judgment, were humbling. On average the experts did little better than simple rules, such as assuming the status quo would continue, and in many areas their accuracy was close to chance. Specialists were often not much better than well-informed generalists when forecasting outside their narrow fields.

But some experts did much better than others, and the difference lay less in what they knew than in how they thought. Borrowing an image attributed to the Greek poet Archilochus ("the fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing"), Tetlock described two styles. Hedgehogs organized everything around one big theory and made bold, confident predictions. Foxes drew on many ideas, were comfortable with doubt, and adjusted their views when the facts changed. The foxes were consistently more accurate. The hedgehogs, ironically, were often the most famous, since bold certainty made for better television.
lesson: Trust forecasters, and train yourself, to think in probabilities, use many sources and change course when evidence shifts. Confident single-theory predictions are more entertaining than accurate.
source: Tetlock, P. E. (2005). Expert Political Judgment: How Good Is It? How Can We Know? Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press.
